Jobs Involving Routine Tasks Aren't Growing

A few years ago I designed a software application that automated the jobs of about 50 people and made them unemployed. The project took 24 months from start until the end of the staggered deployment process and I knew from the first day that most of the people I was working with would be fired.

We gave those people 24 months notice that their jobs would likely become redundant and ran a few brief lunch-time workshops to help them modernize their resumes. I asked for a dozen volunteers to help me with the business systems analysis and testing with the incentive that I'd vouch for them as a referee in modernizing the business.

I was expecting the environment to become hostile as the deployment approached, however during that two year period, most people were able to find new jobs, start new careers, seek training and most were sincerely thankful to leave their horrifically shitty job. They loved the new software application, were excited to have been part of it's development and even more revealed to find a better job. It was a real team-building exercise despite the fact the team was being dismantled: we vetted each other's resumes and celebrated each person who quit because they found a new job and offered support to those who remained.

My point is there is no need to be a Luddite if the transition from low-skilled jobs to automation is managed carefully and the staff are encouraged to prepare.

That said, no amount of Affirmative Action will make some corners of American society productive. In my experience, no amount of training will be sufficient to educate some people to wash their hands after taking a shit and not to urinate in food.
